The Articles of 1896 are reported here, to which the six witnesses of the first Process responded, even though they do not appear materially transcribed in the Process itself. They are now taken from the copy found in the historical Archive of the Institute of the Daughters of St. Anne. Those of 1913 (Proc. pp. 29-69) are omitted, however, since they were never used owing to the suspension of the inquiry. Indeed, the last deposition of that period dates back to 19 November 1907.

(1896; AFSA C3.164)

1. That the truth was and is that, in Albareto, Diocese of Piacenza, Province of Parma, in the district of Borgotaro, on 23 [sic: recte 22] February 1842, Angelo and Domenica Mussi had born to them the Servant of God Sister Anna del Salvatore Orsi, who was the first of nine children. The parents, who were marked by singular piety, wished, before anything else, that the baby, the day after her birth, receive holy baptism, which was administered to her by the Rector of the Parish, Fr. Giovanni Maestri, and she was given the name Marianna, as will be deposed by witnesses well informed and worthy of belief, giving as the ground of their knowledge that it was public and well known, of public voice and repute.

2. That, etc., to the religious upbringing that, with every care, her parents sought to give the Servant of God, she responded with a perfect obedience to her mother, from whom she never parted, seeking to put into practice all those holy teachings that were given her by her every day.

Of a sweet and easily yielding disposition, Marianna bent readily to others' wishes, loving towards the little brothers and sisters born after her, showing every care for them, fond of pious things, and shunning childish amusements, etc.

3. That, etc., when the Servant of God was four years old, she was admitted to receive Confirmation, which Sacrament was administered to her in the Parish Church of Borgotaro by the Bishop of Pontremoli, Msgr. Angelo Orlandi. Soon afterwards, being well instructed in the Catechism, whose explanations she assiduously attended in her Parish, and showing special good sense, she merited being admitted to the Sacred Eucharistic Table, etc.

4. That, etc., the Servant of God grew up very devout, and in household tasks was ready for any command. She especially showed her diligence in caring for her little brothers and sisters, a task that her mother, being occupied at times with other family matters, entrusted entirely to Marianna. She then watched over them attentively, put up with their whims, satisfied their lawful wishes, admonished and instructed them as circumstances required, etc.

5. That, etc., her brothers Luigi and Giovanni having been admitted as day students at the Seminary of Bedonia, the Servant of God had to follow them in order to attend to everything concerning household matters, such as preparing food, caring for the linen, cleaning the house, and even guiding them in place of their mother, who had stayed in Albareto to manage the rest of the large family, etc.

6. That, etc., the Servant of God having completed this task, her two uncles, Don Antonio and Don Luigi Mussi, parish priest the one at Buzzò and the other at Rovinaglia, wished to have her with them, to entrust to her the good running of their households. The young woman complied with her uncles' wish and, going now to one, now to the other, diligently gave her service. But Marianna could not get used to being apart from her Mother and her family, and so decided to return to Albareto, etc.

7. That, etc., the family of Angelo Orsi, having grown excessively large while the father had, to support it, only insufficient means, was forced, in order to seek elsewhere the earnings lacking in Albareto, to sell his property and move his residence and that of the whole family to Centovera, in the Piacenza area, which took place in the year 1863 [sic for 1862]. The Servant of God alone remained in Albareto, in the house of her maternal uncles Francesco and Lorenzo, acting as housekeeper, where, loved and respected for her incomparable goodness, she stayed three years, after which she returned to her family, etc.

8. That, etc., as piety and love for religious practices grew ever more in the young woman, so did her disdain for amusements and worldly things grow in her. Thus, if at times she was obliged to accept invitations from friends or relatives to some family celebration, she would come back so distressed as to weep in the silence of her little room. It also happened, at that time, that she was offered a good marriage proposal, which she refused, saying she did not wish to marry because she felt drawn to the monastic life, etc.

9. That, etc., the Servant of God having made known to a trusted person her intention of becoming a religious in an Institute where she could devote herself to the care of the sick, the Institute of the Daughters of St. Anne, then newly arising, was at once pointed out to her. Marianna remained still some time with her family in order to be more certain of the divine call, and as soon as she had clearly recognised it, she set forth her unchangeable decision to her family, who, grieved at losing so necessary a young woman for their household's work, at first opposed her; but her daughter's pleadings were so many, and the religious feeling in her parents so lively, that they at last gave way, and she was granted what she so anxiously desired, etc.

10. That, etc., on 4 November 1868 the Servant of God, blessed by her grieving parents, left her little village to go to the Institute of the Daughters of St. Anne, already founded three years before. There she began her Postulancy, giving such rare examples of virtue that Mother Rosa, after some months, calling her to herself, told her that the time had come for her to be able to put on the religious habit; on receiving this news Marianna showed such great joy that she seemed almost beside herself, etc.

11. That, etc., on 28 March 1869 took place the ceremony of her Clothing, and the Servant of God received the veil with indescribable gladness of soul. From that day she began her Novitiate, during which she was a most singular example of every virtue. Sent at times to attend some poor sick person, she thanked whoever provided her so great a pleasure, and she was a true angel at the bedside of the poor and unfortunate, etc.

12. That, etc., it being clearly seen by all how greatly useful this new Institute would be to Society, several cities soon sought the work of the Daughters of St. Anne, to relieve the poor sick with free care in their homes and in Hospitals, and to instruct poor children in the nurseries. As this holy institution spread ever more each day, and the number of aspirants grew daily, new personnel were always needed. Thus Sister Anna del Salvatore, who in her few months of novitiate had given clear signs of being accomplished in every virtue, was sent by the Mother House of Piacenza elsewhere, to edify by her conduct, fulfilling the mission God had assigned her. And indeed she so excelled in discharging her office that soon, in that other place too, she was admired and loved by all who knew her, etc.

13. That, etc., the Servant of God's virtues becoming ever more evident, Mother Gattorno, needing a Superior for the founding of a new house, entrusted the difficult task to Sister Anna del Salvatore. She discharged this office in such a way as to be admirable in all her actions. But after some time, her active and intelligent work being needed in another house, the Servant of God was taken from the place where she was and sent to that other new house, etc.

14. That, etc., there too the Servant of God soon showed her zeal for the good of souls, the spirit of charity with which she was filled, the great holiness of her life. But the Superiors judged it right to give Sister Anna another assignment: she was then withdrawn from that house. The Servant of God obeyed and left the Community, after blessing her fellow Sisters, who sobbed at the loss of their affectionate mother. In a short span of time she passed successively from one House to another, wherever her compassionate, intelligent, and diligent work was urgently needed; thus Genoa, Macerata, Naples, Rome, and other cities saw the Servant of God amid sacrifices made to relieve the suffering neighbour, and admired her as an Angel from Paradise, etc.

15. That, etc., in the General Chapter held at the Mother House in Piacenza, attended by all the Superiors of the Order, the Servant of God was elected by unanimous vote as Provincial of all the houses of the Daughters of St. Anne in Sicily. She accepted this grave and difficult charge out of obedience, and discharged it so well that she gave everyone an admirable display of the rare virtues she possessed. Termini Imerese, Trapani, Sambuca di Sicilia, Girgenti (Agrigento), Linguaglossa, Adernò, and very many other Sicilian towns she travelled through out of zeal for her office and to bring comfort to the unfortunate, leaving everywhere an unforgettable memory of her holiness, etc.

16. That, etc., the Servant of God persevered always in the exercise of every virtue, spending every moment of her life benefiting her neighbour in every way, until, exhausted by continual vigils, consumed by fasting and mortifications, worn out by her labours, she flew to Heaven, etc.

De Fide

17. That, etc., the Servant of God Sister Anna del Salvatore firmly believed all that God has revealed to Holy Church, and believed it with full firmness, seeking to instill these truths in others as well. Moreover, she always kept fixed in her mind the thought of God's presence in whatever action she performed, etc.

18. That, etc., the Servant of God showed clearly, from her tenderest years, by what faith she was moved, for at the age of four, on receiving the Sacrament of Confirmation, she presented herself before the Bishop with such modesty and devout feeling that she gave a manifest sign of grasping the full importance of this Sacrament, etc.

19. That, etc., a sign of the Servant of God's faith was her desire to learn Christian Doctrine, the exactness with which she attended the Parish priest's instruction every Sunday, the attention she gave to all religious teaching, so that she soon merited being admitted to the Sacred Eucharistic Table, etc.

20. That, etc., the Servant of God was most punctual in attending the Divine Sacrifice every day and, as far as she could, always took part in sermons, the divine Offices, religious functions, Novenas, and, when the ringing of the bell summoned the faithful to accompany the Blessed Viaticum to some sick person, she hurried eagerly and dutifully to the Church. The great devotion with which she attended all these holy ceremonies was also admirable, etc.

21. That, etc., the Servant of God loved prayer above all things, and spent every moment left free from her duties kneeling at the foot of the altar before the Blessed Sacrament, and so great was the pleasure she found in prayer that, had she been allowed, she would have spent day and night in prayer without ever taking food or rest, etc.

22. That, etc., a sure proof of the Servant of God's most living faith was the deep feeling and the words, all alive with faith, in which she declared herself grateful to God for the gift of faith, and expressed her ineffable sorrow for so many unfortunate souls deprived of the light of faith, the prayers she offered that the faith of Jesus Christ might spread to every remotest corner of the world, and the earnest care with which she urged all whom she could to acknowledge and be grateful to God for so great a benefit, etc.

23. That, etc., the Servant of God had particular devotion for, and venerated, all the mysteries of our Holy Faith, celebrating their solemnities with a more intense practice of virtue and devout preparation; she showed a most intense faith towards the Most Holy Sacrament of the Eucharist and was eager to approach the eucharistic table. She also had a special devotion, which she sought to spread by every means, for the Most Holy Virgin, for St. Anne, of whom she called herself a daughter, and for all the Saints of Paradise, to whom she commended herself in her distresses, etc.

24. That, etc., in the Servant of God there was great respect and veneration for the Supreme Pontiff, whom she knew to hold the place of Christ on earth. She therefore obeyed his decrees, as she scrupulously obeyed all the laws of the Church. She respected priests and all her Superiors, showing herself deferential, obedient, and subject to them in all things, etc.

25. That, etc., she had a most lively feeling of piety and devotion towards the Holy souls in purgatory, for whose relief from the pains they suffer she was altogether eager to gain the holy indulgences, which she held in the highest esteem, and with the greatest zeal she took care that others too should perform meritorious works in suffrage for those holy souls, to whom she was accustomed to turn confidently in every circumstance, always experiencing their ready help, etc.

26. That, etc., the fervour and firmness of the Servant of God's faith was made manifest in the constant effort and the most zealous care she took that her daughters and Sisters, the women and children in her care, the girls or boys in the houses she headed, should be exactly instructed in every Christian duty, in all that Holy Faith teaches us and the Church sets before us to believe; care and zeal that bore the most excellent fruits, etc.

De Spe

27. That, etc., the Servant of God Sister Anna del Salvatore was endowed with a firm hope of attaining, through divine goodness and mercy and through the infinite merits of Jesus Christ, eternal Beatitude. And, animated by this hope, she did everything, undertook everything, bore everything, etc.

28. That, etc., the Servant of God, from girlhood, animated by the hope of eternal goods, despised all the vain things of the world and all the pleasures it offered her. She therefore decided to bid farewell to everyone and withdraw to a monastery, where she would lead a life full of hardship, privation, and toil, etc.

29. That, etc., the Servant of God clearly showed how great in her was the virtue of hope in all the anguish and all the toils she had to bear during her religious life. Indeed, in the difficult offices entrusted to her, she continually ran into obstacles and hindrances that seemed insurmountable: she sometimes saw the Community lacking necessary things, was tormented by sad thoughts, was alarmed by the grave responsibilities entrusted to her; but Sister Anna, always turning to prayer and trusting in God, who could not abandon her, overcame everything, succeeded in everything, even rejoicing in such arduous trials, etc.

30. That, etc., several times the Servant of God suffered the assaults of the infernal enemy, who sought to drive her to despair by making her see the most serious obligations she had to fulfil in religious life, the difficulty of fulfilling them well, and the hell from which she could not escape unless she had perfectly carried out all that was required of her. But she trusted in God, called upon him, and, hoping in the infinite merits of Jesus Christ, did not lose heart, gained courage, and victoriously overcame temptation, etc.

31. That, etc., this beautiful virtue of hers appeared in the last moments of her life, in the tranquility and the smile with which she met death, for she firmly hoped she would go on to enjoy the eternal goods of Paradise.

De Charitate in Deum

32. That, etc., Sister Anna always loved God with her whole heart, with her whole soul, and with all her strength, and always served Him with filial love and with all exactness, seeking nothing but to please Him, having nothing in view but His honour and glory, and used to say to Jesus: "let me follow your holy will in all things and through all things," etc.

33. That, etc., how much she loved God she showed by scrupulously observing all His commandments, the evangelical precepts, and also all the Rules of the Institute, and she showed it by the care she took always to keep far from anything that might, even in the least degree, offend her Lord, etc.

34. That, etc., she showed her charity towards God already in her earliest years, when, having to receive her Jesus in her heart for the first time, with hands joined and eyes fixed on the Sacred Host, she awaited the longed-for moment with such ardour that her interior charity became outwardly visible. All through her life, then, she frequented the Holy Sacraments, which she desired most ardently, etc.

35. That, etc., the charity with which the Servant of God was aglow was seen on the day of her clothing, when, as though in ecstasy and carried away by the thought of becoming the bride of her Jesus, all in tears and with a glowing face, she intoned the Te Deum with her Sisters, etc.

36. That, etc., so great was the fervour that carried her away for Jesus that when she prayed before the Blessed Sacrament, her face all aglow and beside herself, she no longer heard anything happening around her. When she had spent whole days in the gravest toils, at night, while the community slept a peaceful sleep, she would shut herself in the Chapel and there, praying on her knees before the Blessed Sacrament, would spend the whole night happy and in ecstasy in sweet converse with her Jesus, who was her only desire and to whom every aspiration and thought of hers was directed, etc.

37. That, etc., she suffered every pain for love of her God, and so great was her charity that she asked Him for still more pains and trials to bear for Him, saying: "O my Crucified One, I do suffer, it is true, but my suffering is always little compared to the great deal I have made and still make You suffer by my sins, O infinite Goodness, worthy of being loved infinitely. Send me, O Jesus, send me still crueler sorrows, and I, in atonement for my unpardonable faults, will bear them always blessing Your holy will," etc.

38. That, etc., the Servant of God, always faithfully fulfilling every duty, strove ever to progress in the holy exercise of the virtues, so as afterwards to reach that degree of perfection which she attained, etc.

39. That, etc., when, in the last moments of her life, everyone wept around her bed, the Servant of God, all smiling, awaited eagerly the death that, freeing her from the bonds of the body, would let her join her heavenly spouse, whom she loved so greatly and for whom alone she had lived on this earth, etc.

40. That, etc., the love the Servant of God bore her Lord was fed and nourished by the most tender, filial affection she always showed towards His Most Holy Mother, whom she always held also as her own most beloved mother, honouring her and seeing that she was loved and honoured by all, especially in the houses over which she presided, turning to her confidently in every hard circumstance, as the witnesses will explain more fully, etc.

De Charitate in Proximum

41. That, etc., the Servant of God always loved her neighbour as herself, for from girlhood she devoted herself to practicing this virtue in caring for her little brothers and sisters, whom her mother entrusted to her entirely. She watched over them carefully, depriving herself for this of enjoying herself with her other companions of the same age, patiently instructed them, had compassion on their faults, bore their whims, at times defended them against their mother's just severity, pledging herself as surety for their future conduct, admonished them, and guided them attentively along the path of virtue, etc.

42. That, etc., the Servant of God loved her fellow Sisters tenderly, and when she saw one afflicted, sad, weeping at the thought of her distant family or of anything else, Sister Anna, with great tact, drew near to her and, full of concern, sought to restore her calm, speaking to her gently of Paradise, of the comfort she would have in serving Jesus and suffering for Him, counseled her to seek in fervent prayer the means of driving away sadness, urged her to despise the vain things of the world; and she was altogether pleased when she saw that her companion had, through her words, regained her peace, etc.

43. That, etc., she loved the poor and endangered girls who were sheltered in the Religious House. She gladly spent time among them, instructed them, corrected their faults, and would have made any sacrifice to spare them sorrow and hardship. Indeed, since they were maintained partly by very modest fees and partly by alms, Sister Anna tirelessly knocked on the doors of the rich and of benefactors to obtain the help without which those poor girls, whom she tenderly called her little daughters, would have starved; she loved them with a motherly love and gave them the most affectionate care, etc.

44. That, etc., the sick especially experienced how great was the spirit of charity in the Servant of God. Whenever, in keeping with the purpose of the Institute, Sister Anna was sent to the day or night care of some sick person, she rejoiced entirely, was glad, and never ceased thanking the Superiors from whom the order had come. She was not frightened by the squalor and misery of the hovel where she would have to go to spend hour after hour beside the sick lying on filthy straw pallets, without sheets, covered in rags, amid every kind of filth; rather, the Servant of God particularly desired to attend to those sick who caused the most revulsion and disgust, ran to wherever the danger was greatest for her, and with infinite love and patience rendered those unfortunate people every needed service, exhorting them with consoling words to resignation, to patience, to the love of God, so that the sick she attended believed they had an angel at their bedside, etc.

45. That, etc., the Servant of God, being full of charity towards all, had very much at heart the good name of every other person. For this reason not only was she never heard to speak ill of others, but she always found excuses for others' faults and never said a word that could in any way sound like censure or slander of others' conduct, etc.

46. That, etc., the Servant of God's entire life of toil and privation was a continual acting out of the sublime feeling of the most selfless charity. Indeed, she had no other will and no other desire than to sacrifice herself in order to do good to others, which all the towns where Sister Anna lived, even briefly, experienced in abundance, etc.

47. That, etc., the Servant of God's charity never failed for any difficulty or circumstance; rather, it went on growing every day until the last day of her life. It was immense, infinite, extended to every kind of person. She received everyone affably, loved everyone equally, because in everyone she saw and loved God Himself, etc.

De Prudentia

48. That, etc., the Servant of God possessed an admirable prudence joined to a holy simplicity, which she showed throughout her whole life, ever keeping in view, in every action of hers, the glory of God and the attainment of eternal Beatitude, using for this all fitting and suitable means, etc.

49. That, etc., the Servant of God showed, from girlhood, how great her prudence was in bidding farewell to the world and embracing the religious state, which would more easily lead her to possess the eternal Good; and in deciding this she was not content with her first inclinations, but through prayer sought light from God to know His will, and asked counsel of the one who guided her conscience, etc.

50. That, etc., after the Servant of God entered Religion, her prudence showed itself so splendidly that, even before she finished her Novitiate, the work of an active and intelligent person being needed in a new House, the Superiors' choice fell on Sister Anna del Salvatore. From then on, although still very young, she displayed such particular good sense and judgment that she was named Superior in another newly founded House, from which, in a short time, she was sent successively from one House to another, wherever a prudent, diligent, intelligent, and active person was needed, etc.

51. That, etc., the great prudence with which the Servant of God had carried out all the most difficult duties entrusted to her being admired by all, in the General Chapter held at the Mother House in Piacenza, attended by all the Superiors of the Order, Sister Anna del Salvatore was elected by unanimous vote to hold the most important office of Provincial of all the houses of the Daughters of St. Anne in Sicily, etc.

52. That, etc., the prudence with which the Servant of God discharged her office, having won her great esteem and trust with the Administrators of the charitable Houses she directed, she made use of this influence, which she was aware she had over the Administration's disposition, to improve the conditions of the House and of those sheltered there, asking for and obtaining, as occasion allowed, what seemed to her opportune, etc.

53. That, etc., the Servant of God's prudence appeared clearly in all the houses where she was, counseling her fellow Sisters with her wise and prudent judgment, helping them earnestly with exhortations in the difficulties they had to overcome, urging them to sacrifice with holy words and with her admirable example, etc.

De Iustitia

54. That, etc., the Servant of God exercised the virtue of Justice, rendering to all, according to their rank, the honour and respect due to them. Hence she was always most obedient to her Superiors and respectful towards all who had the direction of her, etc.

55. That, etc., she never ceased thanking God for having her born within the bosom of the Catholic Church and for also granting her the most special grace of calling her to the Religious state, and she sought by every means to make herself worthy of so great a favour by a holy life. Hence she continually said she wished to be useful to the Institute that "had given her life," etc.

56. That, etc., seeing at evening that the alms received during the day sufficed to provide for the next day's needs, the Servant of God not only prayed fervently herself for the Benefactors, but called all the Sisters and the young women to her and had them pray for them too, and, speaking of the goodness of God, who never denies His help to those who turn to Him, urged them to thank Him for the many blessings we continually receive from Him, etc.

57. That, etc., the Servant of God, most grateful to her Superiors, thanked them for even the smallest thing, and when the Superior announced to her her imminent clothing, she prostrated herself, deeply moved, before her to attest her gratitude and, promising that she would do everything to make herself worthy of the grace granted her, never ceased thanking her, sobbing with joy, etc.

58. That, etc., Sister Anna observed justice in rendering to God the honour due to Him, seeing that in church everything concerning His worship was orderly, clean, and fitting, and above all that others, whether Sisters or young women, remained there with the utmost respect, the utmost modesty, and edification to others, continually urging the other Sisters to this and diligently watching over it, etc.

59. That, etc., the Servant of God refrained from telling even the smallest lie and observed justice towards her neighbour, never deceiving anyone in any way, never denying anyone their due reward, never harming anyone; all things she never failed to urge upon others too, etc.

De Fortitudine

60. That, etc., the Servant of God was endowed with an admirable fortitude both in undertaking arduous and difficult things and in bearing adversities, and was always constant in the holy exercise of the virtues, ever progressing in them and courageously overcoming every obstacle that rose before her, etc.

61. That, etc., the Servant of God showed this virtue already from girlhood, when her family, its means harmed and finding itself in the greatest straits, she herself showed herself good and affectionate in every circumstance, seeking thus to ease her family's sufferings by her love and diligence at work, keeping an ever cheerful disposition even when the poverty and distress in which she saw her family would have made her shed bitter tears; for although she did not show it, in her heart she grieved greatly for her parents and her brothers and sisters, etc.

62. That, etc., great was the Servant of God's fortitude when she had to part from her parents, whom she loved tenderly and would see no more, in order to go to the Religious Institute, etc.

63. That, etc., the Servant of God had to suffer terrible struggles against the devil, who tormented her, tempting her in a thousand ways against her vocation both before she embraced religious life and afterwards, frightening her with the duties she had to fulfil, and especially, when she was elected Superior and then Provincial, made the obstacles seem insurmountable to her, the difficulties of that office she had to discharge scrupulously most serious, the new anguish that always and everywhere awaited her, and exaggerated her situation in order to turn her from the right path and rob her of courage; but the Servant of God, unyielding in her will and trusting in the Lord, won and overcame these dreadful battles, etc.

64. That, etc., the Servant of God was strong in bearing all the tribulations, both inward and outward, that beset her at every turn; indeed, she did not let on at all what she was suffering, neither to the Superiors nor to the Sisters; but, always cheerful, lighthearted, and serene in spirit, she often exclaimed: "Jesus, let me suffer more." How much she had to bear was not heard from her own lips, but was learned from others who told of it. Going out begging alms, she was several times insulted, scorned, and heaped with abuse, and every day she returned, smiling, to those who had mistreated her, etc.

65. That, etc., the Servant of God had to suffer reproofs and ill-treatment within the Community itself on account of her great zeal and effort for charity towards her neighbour and for the good of the Institute, treatment that was afterwards acknowledged as unjust by the very persons who caused it and from whom it came, and the Servant of God's patience was greatly admired.

66. That, etc., Sister Marianna gave proof of her fortitude in bearing the pains and discomforts of her last illness, and in facing death with admirable tranquility at the young age of 40, herself consoling the sisters who, while she was dying, wept around her bed, etc.

De Temperantia

67. That, etc., the Servant of God was most austere in food, for already in her earliest years, while still with her family, she was seen to eat even the hens' mash; and once a religious, she ate only once a day, feeding on a few vegetables and wilted greens sprinkled with a little water, things she called exquisite, and she used to tell how, when she was with her family, she had grown used to such foods and found her pleasure in them, concluding by saying: "I have always been a little beast." And when she was sent to keep vigil attending the sick, out of obedience she took coffee, but made it with the soot she scraped from the pots. However many feast days there were, she never took fruit, nor sweets, nor any other food beyond the ordinary, etc.

68. That, etc., the Servant of God, just as she was temperate in food, was likewise temperate in rest. After whole days spent in toil and nights spent keeping vigil to care for the sick, when she returned to the Community she never went to rest, so that, although she herself had seen to it that the other Religious had a good bed, she herself never had one; and to anyone who urged her that she too should rest, she answered that she had no need to lie down in order to rest and sleep, and that a bed would therefore be, for her, something superfluous and a luxury, since she made no use of one, adding: "If I were to fall ill, I would surely find some kind Sister who would give up her bed to me; but meanwhile, thank God, I enjoy excellent health, so here is my bed" — and she would point to a chair — "it serves me marvelously!", etc.

69. That, etc., having been caught several times late at night in prayer, and being told to go and rest, she would answer that it was not yet late and that she had to stay there to keep Jesus company, who was alone in the Chapel, etc.

70. That, etc., as much as she was indulgent, compassionate, solicitous, and full of concern for her fellow Sisters, that they should eat, take the necessary rest, and watch over their health, so much was she rigorous, severe, and cruel towards herself, subjecting her frail body to every toil without granting it afterwards any relief, neither of food nor of rest, etc.

71. That, etc., the Servant of God having once arrived at the Community after a long journey, still fasting, all the Sisters gathered around her to give her something to eat; but she wanted nothing of what had been prepared for her, taking only out of obedience a drop of wine, which made her unwell all night long, as always happened to her whenever, in order to obey, she tasted even the smallest thing beyond her usual vegetables, etc.

72. That, etc., very great in the Servant of God was her desire for penance. She tormented her most innocent body with the most atrocious disciplines, tormented it with hairshirts and small chains, tortured it with little iron nets that had some points on their underside, which she also wore on her thighs; these instruments were several times discovered by her fellow Sisters, as happened one day when, the doctor having to come into her room, and she not having time to remove those instruments of penance, one of them was found on the floor and picked up by a sister, to the immense distress of the Servant of God, etc.

73. That, etc., on Fridays the Servant of God seemed to torment her body all the more with these hairshirts, for it was observed that on those days, whether rising, sitting, or moving, the signs of the great sufferings she endured appeared on her face, etc.

74. That, etc., the Servant of God's Temperance showed itself excellent in the perfect mastery she achieved over herself and her passions, such that her face betrayed no stirring of anger or unmastered passion even in the most difficult, arduous, and unforeseen cases, always keeping the loveliest calm, with which she showed she had conquered herself, as the witnesses will explain with similar facts, etc.

De votorum observantia

De Paupertate

75. That, etc., the Servant of God despised all worldly things and was a most ardent lover of poverty. This was evident from her clothing, about which she never gave a thought. The more patched her habit was, the better she liked it, and the Very Reverend Mother once had to oblige her to put on a new tunic, since in the one she had worn for many, many years the patches and mends lay one upon another. She would even have gone about with her toes showing through her shoes had her fellow Sisters not taken care to change them; and even then, as soon as she noticed the change, she would at once give the new ones to another Sister, keeping the old ones for herself, etc.

76. That, etc., the Servant of God would never have allowed herself the slightest waste. She called herself owner of nothing, considering herself merely the keeper of the Community's goods, and in this she was most scrupulous, distributing at once, as soon as she returned home, everything that had been given her in alms. She kept account of everything, and so as not to throw away that little scrap of wick taken from a new candle, she made use of it, dyeing it yellow, to make the stamens of artificial flowers, etc.

77. That, etc., everything around the Servant of God or belonging to her breathed poverty; hence not only her clothing but her very room was so wretched that it lacked even the most necessary things, such as a bed, which Sister Anna did not have, saying that for her it would have been a luxury, etc.

78. That, etc., having once arrived at the Community, all gay and smiling, she told the Sisters that she had travelled with her Companion in the livestock car, because she did not have enough money to travel comfortably, etc.

79. That, etc., that spirit of poverty which she possessed she sought to instill in all her fellow Sisters as well, and she wanted them to come to table as poor little women coming to receive alms, and she was altogether pleased to go from house to house asking for offerings, so as to be able to say that she lived by begging, etc.

De Castitate

80. That, etc., the Servant of God was always most chaste and sought, by every means, to preserve this beautiful virtue, keeping every shadow of impurity far from herself, having become a Religious in order always to keep intact the lovely lily of chastity, etc.

81. That, etc., the Servant of God clearly made known, in every one of her actions, the love she bore this virtue. Always most reserved, never once did she let slip an act or a word that was less than proper, and nothing could ever be caught in her that betrayed, even in the slightest, the innocence of her heart, virgin of every human malice, etc.

82. That, etc., the Servant of God, in order to keep herself always pure and unspotted, continually exercised herself in prayer, fed herself always on the Bread of Angels, and kept her flesh subject through disciplines, mortifications, and fasts, etc.

83. That, etc., the Servant of God never ceased to commend this beautiful virtue and urged it upon the Sisters, that they should guard it jealously, keeping especially their eyes in check, and that they should pray to the Virgin Mother of God to preserve for them the precious treasure of holy purity, etc.

De Oboedientia

84. That, etc., among all the fine qualities and virtues that adorned the Servant of God, obedience to her Superiors shone out in a special way. From the time she entered the Community, the Mistress's will was sacred to her, and every wish of hers was a command, so that she would never have drawn back before any obstacle whenever she had to carry out an order from any of her Superiors, and she obeyed gladly, without any regret, a smile on her lips, raising no objection whatsoever, since she imagined she was obeying God Himself, etc.

85. That, etc., even when the Servant of God was Superior and then Provincial of the houses in Sicily, she gave an admirable example of obedience, for, showing herself a most faithful daughter of the Most Reverend Mother, she saw only through her eyes and heard only through her ears. A single sign manifesting that mother's will was enough for it to be carried out at once by the Servant of God, who, moreover, made a most special study of anticipating her very wishes, etc.

86. That, etc., the Servant of God gave an example of obedience when, obliged by the Mother to take foods different from those her stomach had long since grown accustomed to, that is, vegetables and greens, Sister Anna said not a word and ate, but then felt so unwell that she had to bring it all up again, with great pain. Yet she suffered all the while content, knowing she had done her Mother's will and satisfied her wishes, which were law to her, etc.

87. That, etc., the Servant of God, lying ill with fever in Palermo, received an order from the Mother, who knew nothing of her illness, to go urgently attend to a matter at the Institute of Trapani. By virtue of obedience she at once rose from her bed with a fever of 104°F, went to Trapani, where she stayed one day, the time needed to carry out the task entrusted to her, and then returned to Palermo in such a dreadful state as to cause alarm, and, having taken to her bed, never rose again, etc.

88. That, etc., also in her last illness this beautiful virtue stood out in her, for she submitted fully to everything ordered of her by those who treated and attended her, even when her own will would have resolutely opposed it, etc.

89. That, etc., the Servant of God so observed all the Rules of the Institute that not a single point of them was neglected by her, wishing that the other Sisters too should do so and urging them to it; and the Sisters who lived with Sister Anna said it would be an extraordinary grace for them if they could manage even distantly to imitate her, etc.

De Humilitate

90. That the Servant of God shone most highly in the Virtue of Humility by the utterly low regard she had for her own person; hence, to anyone who told her it would be impossible to replace her adequately, she would reply that she was the last of the Daughters of St. Anne and that whoever replaced her would do better than she; thus, when they called her by the title of Superior, she would say: "the Superiors of this House are St. Anne and Our Lady; they rule and govern it: I am a mere nothing." Moreover she judged herself with the greatest severity, accusing herself of being full of faults and considering herself, in every act of hers, deserving of pity, and she used to say: "Everyone is good, kind, and holy except me, who am a very wicked woman," etc.

91. That, etc., she spoke humbly with all her companions and welcomed every correction with gratitude. If it happened that she made a mistake in doing something, she at once blamed her own ignorance and begged whoever it might be to give her suggestions; whereas, if she had to give suggestions to others, she did so with such humility that no one was ever mortified by it. If she was chosen for some office, she never ceased begging the Mistress to choose others more capable than she, and she did all this not for show but because she was inwardly convinced she was the most ignorant and inept of all the young women. Not obtaining what she asked, she prayed to God to help her carry out well the task entrusted to her, etc.

92. That, etc., out of love for this virtue, the Servant of God practiced all the lowliest offices and services, never feeling the least repugnance, and always with a cheerful and serene spirit; and, finding herself in a house, which the witnesses will specify, where Mass could not be had every morning, she would send the sisters to church to hear it before going herself, while meanwhile at home she attended to the most menial chores, such as sweeping the rooms, making the beds, and dusting the furniture, etc.

93. That, etc., as solicitous as the Servant of God was for all the Sisters, continually seeing that they lacked nothing, just so little did she care for herself, and she never asked anything for herself; and when the Superior asked her, "Sister, do you need anything?" she would humbly answer: "A little love of God, Superior," etc.

94. That, etc., so great was the love the Servant of God had for humility that one could clearly see also outwardly the pain and distress she felt within whenever she heard anyone praise her, protesting then against such praise and heaping upon herself the most humbling epithets with all possible energy, trying to persuade everyone of the contrary, etc.

95. That, etc., the Servant of God delighted in being humbled and reproved, even unjustly, just as she delighted in receiving refusals and, at times, scorn, when going from house to house, to the doors of the rich, to ask an offering for the Community; she was altogether content with these humiliations, thinking that Jesus had suffered for us something far more humiliating and ignominious, etc.

96. That, etc., the Servant of God so loved the virtue of humility that her conferences always concerned this virtue, and, continually urging the Sisters always to hold it dear, she taught them always to keep themselves last of all, always to humble themselves, since God is often wont to bring down pride, etc.

De Donis Supernaturalibus et Miraculis in vita

97. That, etc., Sister Anna del Salvatore was adorned by God with supernatural gifts. Indeed, she was seen to rise in ecstasy from the ground while praying; at other times, while at prayer, even when called and shaken several times, she did not hear; at other times she was heard as though speaking with Jesus in a mysterious language that could not be understood, things the witnesses will specify well. She also had the gift of tears, the reading of hearts, and, several times, the Sisters who were with her saw her disappear without being able to find her again, etc.

98. That, etc., the Servant of God was endowed with the gift of Prophecy, that is, she had knowledge of distant things. Thus, while in Piacenza, she foretold that she would soon be sent from there to another house and would see a certain person, as the witnesses will specify, which indeed came to pass. And a week before she fell gravely ill, she went to another house, which the witnesses will specify, to see a sister long ill, and said to her: "Courage, sister, for you will not die now, but both you and I have little time left to live." Which was fulfilled, etc.

99. That, etc., to another Sister who, in order not to cause her distress, wished to hide from her the very grave illness of another Sister, the Servant of God said frankly: "Have no doubt, sister, that gravely ill sister will not die; I shall die; but she will recover, and soon." And so it was, etc.

100. That, etc., God, through His Servant while still living, deigned to work wonders. Sister Anna once took a postulant to an aunt, who gave her niece an envelope containing 80 lire. On arriving home, the said Postulant gave the Servant of God that money received from her Aunt. But Sister Anna, after looking at it, exclaimed: "But this is not the money I need; I am short by more than double at least." Meanwhile she gave the envelope back to the young woman and, taking her to the church, told her to put it behind the Altar Card and urged her to pray a great deal. She then left the church and, when she returned two hours later, the envelope was found with the money increased by 200 lire, etc.

101. That, etc., a young woman who was in the Boarding House which the witnesses will specify, and for whom a pious person paid the board, having one day learned of the death of this charitable Lady, was so distraught that, no longer reasoning, in the height of her anguish, at night put some matches in a glass of water and swallowed the poisonous drink. Hearing the young woman's cries and learning what had happened, the frightened Sisters ran to the Superior, Sister Anna, who, although lying gravely ill in bed, leapt up, ran to the unfortunate girl, and, seeing her near death, threw herself on her knees with arms outstretched in a cross, praying fervently to the Crucified One. The priest and the doctor had already been sent for, but when they arrived the dying girl was saved, for, once the Servant of God's prayers were finished, the poisoned girl had miraculously vomited up all the poison, etc.

102. That, etc., at this so unexpected recovery, all the sisters, amazed, believed it a miracle God had worked through the Superior's intercession, and the priest and the doctor looked at one another in astonishment, seeking and asking for an explanation of so unprecedented an event, which humanly could never have happened, etc.

De fama sanctitatis in vita

103. That, etc., for the sublime and heroic virtues in which the Servant of God shone at all times, she was always universally held by all in a particular esteem as a Saint, and had a great reputation for holiness among all who knew her or heard tell of her, etc.

104. That, etc., very soon the fame of her holiness, passing from mouth to mouth from the hovels where she went to attend the poor sick, reached even into the mansions, and everyone, poor and rich alike, enthused by the wonders of such great charity and self-denial of hers, began to call Sister Anna an angel sent from heaven to comfort human misery, a saint of Paradise, an admirable example of virtue, etc.

105. That, etc., the Servant of God, through her virtues, won such great esteem and respect from the whole population that people continually flocked to her to ask advice in difficult matters, and to be set at peace by her holy words in their anguish and troubles, both material and spiritual, etc.

106. That, etc., from the high regard in which the Superior was held there came great benefit to the house, for when she came seeking alms, no one dared refuse an offering to one who sacrificed herself out of charity for others; so that, whereas the Community had often lacked what it needed, it afterwards had not only to meet every need but also to provide a modest furnishing for the house. All, admiring the Servant of God's holiness, would have done anything for her; hence the poor prayed for the good Daughters of St. Anne, the rich were lavish with every consideration towards them, and everyone considered it a true honour to be able to guess the Superior's wishes in order to satisfy them, etc.

107. That, etc., for her special gifts the Servant of God was admired and respected by the Sisters and by all the Superiors of the houses to which she had been sent with the office of Superior. Finally, made Provincial of all the houses of Sicily, she had gained such prestige with everyone that it was enough for her to speak for not only all the Sisters but also the Priests and lay people who dealt with her to feel drawn towards her with deep reverence and moved to satisfy her wishes, etc.

108. That, etc., this very great reputation for holiness the Servant of God enjoyed not only among poor or common people, but among everyone, including clergy and persons eminent in rank, standing, and learning, as the witnesses will specify. And this reputation was constant, never contradicted, interrupted, or diminished; rather, ever growing, it lasted until the precious death of the Servant of God, etc.

De pretioso obitu

109. That, etc., the Servant of God Sister Anna del Salvatore, seized by an inward illness and a very high fever, had to take to her bed, and every remedy was judged useless. Meanwhile the illness made rapid progress, and the Mother General was at once informed, to her very great sorrow. Meanwhile she lay in bed, patient in the sufferings of her illness, loving and affectionate towards her sisters, solicitous for all of them, who vied with one another to be around her in order to admire, even in those moments, her singular virtues and take them as example, etc.

110. That, etc., among all the virtues shown during the Servant of God's illness, obedience stood out. For while she lay gravely ill in bed, the Mother General, by telegram, ordered her, as a test of her virtue, to receive Communion in the Chapel with her fellow Sisters and remain working with them the whole day. The Servant of God rose, tottering, and made her Holy Communion, and it happened wonderfully that from that moment the fever ceased and such an improvement began in her that she was able to stay out of bed for three or four days; only when eating would she say: "This goes in, but it doesn't come out again," which the Sisters took as a joke, etc.

111. That, etc., the terrible illness of peritonitis showed itself, and, with no time to inform the Mother General again, the Servant of God found herself at the point of death. Every day a crowd of people, tears in their eyes, came to ask news of the dying woman, and the sisters, pressed close around her bed, lavished her with affectionate care, to which she responded by affectionately squeezing now one hand, now another, in a sign of gratitude, etc.

112. That, etc., the illness growing ever worse, she asked for and received the Blessed Viaticum. The priest then entered, followed by all the weeping Sisters with lighted candles, and the Servant of God, sitting up in bed with hands joined and eyes raised to heaven, smiled; and, when the Sacred Host was brought close to her lips, a ray of light was seen reflected on her face, which seemed that of a Saint, etc.

113. That, etc., the Sisters, overcome with grief around the Superior's bed, kneel and beg forgiveness for the faults they committed against her. The dying woman opens her eyes, looks at them with a smile, and, her strength failing, asks the Confessor to bless the Sisters in her place. Then, in a voice that grows ever fainter, she commends to them the exact observance of the Rules and love for the Mother; then, her breathing growing ever more laboured, stammering with difficulty Jesus, Joseph, Mary, and St. Anne, and the name of Mother, she sweetly gives up her soul to God. It was the 5th of June 1885, she being 40 years of age, etc.

114. That, etc., the Mother General, having no time to reach Sister Anna, on learning the sad news sent her the blessing by telegram; but even the telegram arrived when the Servant of God had already breathed her last, etc.

115. That, etc., as soon as the bitter loss of the Servant of God became known, everyone flocked to the house, hoping to venerate her blessed body, obtain some relic, or get hold of some object she had owned; and some recalled the benefits received from her, others her words, others still recalled and praised her virtues. Meanwhile the Prince and Princess of Fitalia ordered that the Servant of God's body be photographed at once, at their own expense. The mortal remains of Sister Anna del Salvatore were buried on the evening of 7 June, that is, two days after her death, etc.

De Fama Sanctitatis post obitum

116. That, etc., the reputation for holiness the Servant of God enjoyed even while living became even greater after her death. Thus, as soon as she died, the public newspapers, from whose passages praising the deceased Servant of God the Postulator asks that extracts be inserted into the Process records, spoke of her at length, praised her virtues, and held her up to all as an example. And while the Mother General and the Institute arranged that the funeral rites prescribed by the Rules be held for the deceased, and that her soul be prayed for in every Community, Palermo prepared to give the deceased the fullest testimony of its great veneration for her, etc.

117. That, etc., the solemn funeral the city of Palermo held for the Servant of God, which took place on 15 June in the Oratory of the Central House of Sicily, within the Briuccia Palace, proved most moving. Inscriptions recalling Sister Anna's distinguished virtues adorned the Chapel all round, entirely covered with mourning veils. An urn covered in velvet and gold stood in the centre, at whose foot wreaths of flowers were laid, etc.

118. That, etc., all the noble and devout ladies of Palermo flocked to pay that final tribute of admiration to one who had been so dear to them and whom they always held to be a saint, and Msgr. Gaetano Gabrielle delivered a eulogy on the deceased's virtues, holding her up to all as a rare example of humility, of charity, of every virtue, etc.

119. That, etc., the Servant of God's reputation for holiness growing greater every day, at the request of the whole populace the Cardinal Archbishop Celesia ordered that Sister Anna del Salvatore's body be placed in a place of deposit, according to the prescriptions of the Holy Roman Church. This holy ceremony was carried out at the Cemetery of St. Ursula, in the presence of Msgr. Giovanni Cirino, Archbishop of Ancyra and Vicar General of the Archdiocese of Palermo, many other prelates, the Chancellor of the Curia, and a numerous company of the Daughters of St. Anne, together with the Mother General herself, come from Rome, etc.

120. That, etc., on the opening of the coffin containing the Servant of God's remains, the emotion was general, and everyone crowded around it, some to kiss the hands of that body, others to touch it with rosaries and other devotional objects, others still to gaze upon it and praise Sister Anna's holiness, etc.

121. That, etc., the verification concluded, the Servant of God's body, with a parchment on which her life was briefly written, was shut in a new coffin with the archiepiscopal seals, and a record was drawn up of everything. The ceremony concluded with the unbloody sacrifice of the Mass, celebrated by the Reverend Parish Priest Palazzotto, etc.

122. That, etc., very many are the requests made from various places and cities, both near and distant, for some relic, image, or account of the Servant of God's life, and these requests go on increasing every day, and such a reputation did not arise from rumours among the people or from other human circumstances, but solely from the heroic virtues of Sister Anna del Salvatore, etc.

123. That, etc., this reputation for holiness exists not only among the ignorant or common people, but among every class of person, so that rich and poor, noble and common, lay and clergy, respectable in rank, learning, and dignity, venerate Sister Anna, and this reputation has never been interrupted or contradicted; rather, growing ever greater and spreading ever to new places and cities, there is a common desire to see the Servant of God upon the altars with the pronouncement of the Holy See, etc.

De Miraculis post obitum

124. That, etc., the Lord, after the death of His Servant, in order to glorify her still further, deigned to work, through her intercession, very many graces and miracles, and, through invocation of her, through the application of her relics, and through her images, most grave and incurable sick persons were instantly healed, the most atrocious pains were stopped, and comfort was found in distress, etc.

125. That, etc., the Community of the Briuccia House in Palermo finding itself in the direst want, and having to send some sisters to Naples, the Provincial Sister Anna Battistina ordered the Sisters to go to the Chapel and pray to Sister Anna del Salvatore, that she might come to their aid in this need. Meanwhile the said Superior, with Sister Anna Macrina, went to Mrs. Florio's house to ask her for four free places to Naples. But the Sisters had not yet even voiced this wish when the lady sent for her husband, who spontaneously granted not four but six free places, etc.

126. That, etc., Sister Anna Battista Cusmano, a Novice at the House in Rome, from the first days after her clothing suffered such a stomach ailment, as the witnesses will specify, that she found relief in no remedy, and was pained by the fear of perhaps being sent back by the Institute as unfit. Advised to turn to Sister Anna del Salvatore, the poor sick woman began a novena, and on the evening of the first day a quite noticeable improvement appeared in her, and that night, after so many sleepless nights, falling asleep, she dreamed of three nuns who asked her why she was crying. The sick woman answered: "I want to see St. A. del Salvatore to ask her for a grace." She then appeared, and the Novice told her of the illness she had and the anguish that tormented her at perhaps having to leave the Institute. "No" (answered Sister Anna del Salvatore), "the Holy Mother does not wish it," and, touching and pressing her stomach, "you have nothing" (she added), "be obedient," and vanished. The next morning, waking at the rising bell, Sister A. Battista found herself perfectly cured, and from that day had no more trouble at all, etc.

127. That, etc., Sister A. Cunegonda Benini lay gravely ill with Angina in the Hospital of Palermo. After many remedies were tried in vain, Dr. Mondini, after several days, decided to perform an incision on her. The poor sick woman was so frightened that she turned to St. Anna del Salvatore, fervently commending herself to her and promising her three days of fasting on bread and water if she obtained for her the grace of being spared the incision. Indeed, the doctor, returning the next day for the said operation, found it entirely unnecessary, for the gravely ill woman was perfectly cured, and he remained astonished, since such a thing could not happen by human means, etc.

128. That, etc., in September 1887, cholera having broken out in Agira, Mrs. Scilla and Antonina Ragonese were struck down by the illness so suddenly that there was no longer any hope of life. But upon the Servant of God being invoked, as the witnesses will duly relate, they were perfectly cured, etc.

129. That, etc., the Reverend Fr. Gagliani affirms he has received many graces from the Servant of God and has chosen her as his special advocate before the Most High. Thus the witnesses will relate many, many other wondrous happenings and benefits obtained through her, to show how powerful Sister Anna del Salvatore's intercession is before God, and how devotion towards her, and the practice of invoking her in need and distress, spreads ever more, etc.

130. That, etc., the Provincial Sister Anna Battistina Bertuzzi, during her stay in Terranova, developed an extremely painful femoral hernia, whose symptoms were most alarming, as the witnesses will describe exactly, both from their own observation and from having heard it from others, especially physicians or surgeons. An operation had to be performed, there being no other way of hoping for a cure. Meanwhile prayers were offered to the Servant of God, and the sick woman, having with great confidence placed on the affected spot a piece of Sister Anna's veil, felt something like a knot loosen at the place where the hernia had formed, and was instantly cured, as the witnesses will take care to relate in detail and at length, both concerning this and the other miracles, always reporting the type of illness, its course, the care given, the improvement or worsening these produced, the judgment made of them by physicians (whom the undersigned Postulator asks be examined) or other competent persons, the invocation made to the Servant of God, the instant improvement or instant cure that followed upon that invocation, the circumstances of the cure obtained, and all those circumstances serving to set the fact in full light and beyond all doubt and dispute.

WITNESS I
His Excellency the Most Reverend IGNAZIO ZUCCARO

Procedural scope: From Session IV of 25 April 1898 (Process p. 113) to Session VII of 29 April 1898 (Proc. p. 132).

Name, date and place of birth: Ignazio Zuccaro, born in Palermo in 1840.

State and profession: Bishop of Caltanissetta.

Quality of the witness: Eyewitness.

Witness's age when he knew the Servant of God: 40 years.

Servant of God's age when the witness knew her: 38 years.

Witness's age at the time of deposition: 58 years.

Length of acquaintance and its reason: The witness knew the Servant of God from the arrival of the Daughters of St. Anne in Palermo, since, wishing to establish a house of Sisters for home care of the sick, he had a group of six brought there, among them the Servant of God, who acted as Superior. To meet the needs of the community, the witness visited the Servant of God almost daily.

Observations on the witness, the scope, and the content of the deposition: The witness's standing, and the frequent contact he had with the Servant of God in the last five years of her life, give particular weight to his deposition, in which he reports concrete facts, known by direct observation, that highlight especially the Servant of God's humility and desire for self-concealment.

§ 1
General information on the witness.

Ad 2 interr., proc. pag. 113, testis respondit: My name is Ignazio Zuccaro, son of the late Vincenzo, 58 years old, born in Palermo, Bishop of Caltanissetta.

Ad 6: No one has instructed or induced me, either by hope of gain or fear of harm; I have resolved to testify in this Cause solely for the glory of God.

§ 2
Scope of knowledge.

Ad 7: I have known the Servant of God Sister Anna del Salvatore Orsi since the first establishment of the Daughters of St. Anne in Palermo, on the occasion when, wishing to found a house of Sisters to attend to the sick at home, I had a small group of six brought to Palermo, among whom was the Servant of God we are dealing with, who acted as Superior. To meet the needs of the Community, then in its founding stage, I visited the Servant of God almost daily. This goes back to May 1880.

§ 3
Respectful opinion of the Servant of God.

Ad 8: Towards the Servant of God I have always had a respectful opinion: as for any wishes or concerns about her beatification, I defer entirely to the judgment of the Church.

§ 4
The Servant of God always inclined to piety.

Ad 10: After her death, having asked others, I heard it said that she had always been inclined to piety and desirous of embracing some religious Institute.

§ 5
Various places where she worked and reputation for extraordinary charity.

Ad 14: I know she was in Piacenza, Perugia, Ovada, and then finally in Palermo, where she died and where she governed as Superior with great prudence and charity until her death; everywhere she was sent in obedience to the Mother General; elsewhere I do not know in what capacity, but certainly in Palermo as Superior and foundress, where she won a reputation for admirable life and extraordinary charity.

§ 6
Grave persecution and heroic patience in bearing it.

Ad 15: On account of my frequent visits I was able to learn from the older Sisters that, before coming to Palermo, the Servant of God had suffered a most grave persecution in the Community; and, if I remember rightly, she was on the point of being expelled from the Congregation: a persecution she bore with humility and heroic patience. The Lord, however, allowed her innocence to be recognised afterwards, and her virtue was admired by the whole community, to the point of her being held a saint.

§ 7
Always observed the law of God and the rule.

Ad 16: I never had occasion to observe any failing with regard to the law of God, the precepts of the Church, or likewise her rule. This opinion was general in the Community of Sisters.

Ad 17: Concerning this article, I can say first of all, in general, that she was most observant, and in no ordinary way, of the Christian virtues.

§ 8
Practiced the virtues in no ordinary way.
§ 9
Faith tested amid dryness of spirit.

In particular, then, I understand with regard to Faith that she exercised it continually in the presence of God, the night not excepted; although by various devices she sought to conceal herself. Of many things I was myself a witness, but of many others I heard from the Sisters, who, often without meaning to, despite her prohibitions, let it be seen. I know that Our Lord trained her through spiritual dryness, and once, catching her in such a state and, to encourage her, comforting her by saying that the Lord, when He hides, is near to us, she answered at once, without having time to reflect: "And then why does He make Himself known?!"

§ 10
Trust in Providence.

As for Hope, I can say nothing particular, although in general I can affirm her immense trust in divine Providence: so much so that she never grew anxious over life's urgent needs, giving no importance to the money she received.

§ 11
Charity towards God and self-concealment.

Charity towards God. As to charity towards God, it seemed to me truly profound, from what I gathered from what I said above: indeed, I consider that it was not ordinary, for she let nothing of her interior show, but what I could grasp from certain expressions of hers. For with priests she did not reveal herself, out of a spirit of humility and deep respect, rather expecting from them some word of the spirit.

§ 12
Charity towards the neighbour as to the spirit.
§ 13
Charity towards the neighbour as to the body.

Proc. p. 118: As to charity towards the neighbour, I distinguish between charity as to the spirit and charity as to the body. As to the first, much could be said; but I recall that once, obliged by obedience to accompany a sister from Palermo to Trapani, she went, even though running a very high fever: she then brought the sister back to Palermo, and would not leave her there, for fear some spiritual harm might befall her. This was told to me by the Sister herself, named Sister Anna M. Grazia, who added that Sister Anna del Salvatore had reached the station to return to Palermo, and from there, as though inspired, turned back to the house, saying: no, I will not leave her at all. In general I can say that she had great zeal for souls, and spared no toil or suffering in order to do good to souls. As to the body, one could never finish praising her: she was always ready to keep vigil in attending the sick, even to spare the Sisters. It is also known, and I always heard it said, how she would get up at night to do the Sisters' washing, to spare those who should have done it. This seemed remarkable, because it seemed impossible that so much work could be done in a single night; indeed, those obliged to go at the appointed hour, that is, very early, to the laundry, found, to their amazement, everything already done. I also recall that once, perhaps in winter, having arrived in Palermo at a late hour, having climbed the stairs of the house, so as not to disturb the Sisters she stayed outside after having knocked softly and not having been heard, because the Sisters had not been forewarned of her arrival. She also chose for herself the most repugnant sick, whether from sores or for some other reason; and the sick preferred to be attended or treated by her because she had a quite special way of treating them, which I do not know how to account for.

§ 14
Chose the most repugnant sick for herself.
§ 15
Prudence.

As to the cardinal virtues.

On Prudence: Here I believe fits the fact I narrated above, concerning Sister Anna M. Grazia, she being very young and quite attractive in appearance. She was prudent in governing the Community as a simple Superior of the House of the nurse-sisters, and still more so afterwards when, as Provincial Superior, she governed all the houses of Sicily.

§ 16
Justice.

As to Justice: I recall nothing in particular; but I can assure you I never heard anything to the contrary.

§ 17
Temperance.

Temperance: here I say that her life was admirable for its penance, and also for the skill with which she hid it. Visiting the house, I heard that she never ate meat or appetising food; and I have reason to believe she fed on nothing but greens.

§ 18
Fortitude on every occasion of life.

Fortitude: This virtue accompanied her in every act of her life, not only in the exercise of the virtues but also in adversities and persecutions, even unto death.

§ 19
Humility, her characteristic virtue.

Of the other virtues.

On humility I can say that this virtue was her hallmark: the very word Pride filled her with horror, unable as she was to believe one could be guilty of it.

§ 20
Utterly poor.
§ 21
Chastity.

Poverty: she was most poor in spirit, always choosing the worst things for herself, preferring to give the best to the Sisters: so much so that the Sisters themselves had to force her to use something of better quality. I recall that she turned to me so the Sisters would not force her, using as a pretext that the most unsuitable thing was more convenient for her. I also recall that, to meet the needs of the newly founded Community, I once offered her some money: but she, on an occasion when she had no need of it, refused, answering with these words: "Father, having no need of it, to accept it would seem to me greed."

Chastity: She was most modest in all her actions, and no one could ever have the slightest suspicion of wrongdoing regarding her conduct, even though she was in the midst of the exercise of public charity.

§ 22
Obedience.

Obedience: I said above that out of obedience she accompanied the Sister to Trapani while burning with fever. On returning she took to her bed. Then, out of obedience to the Mother General, who had written to her about it, she, in this grave state of health, as I was told, rose from bed and went to the chapel to pray, the Mother General hoping for her recovery; instead, a few days later she died.

§ 23
Mortification practiced in heroic degree.

Ad 18: It is certain that her virtues were not of an ordinary degree: but, owing to the Servant of God's continual self-concealment, I cannot say precisely to what degree her virtues reached. There was much heroism in general: in particular it seems to me that mortification truly reached the heroic degree in her; the desire to suffer was something most ardent in her. This I know from so many very small facts that I cannot relate in detail. The same I can say of obedience, as I narrated above. As for the concept of heroism in virtue, I understand a virtue that surpasses the ordinary and perseveres even unto death.

§ 24
Foretold her own death.

Ad 20: As to this article, I answer that I do not know whether the Servant of God had heavenly gifts and charisms, precisely because, as I have always said, one of the Servant of God's chief virtues was to conceal herself entirely. However, if it may serve as evidence of her spirit of prophecy, I bring forward one fact: in her last illness, when her death was not yet feared, another religious at the same time being afflicted with typhoid fever, to whom I myself had administered the Blessed Viaticum, the Servant of God, who constantly asked about the sick sister, on hearing that she was not gravely ill, answered at once: "You are hiding the truth: but I tell you she will live and I shall die." Indeed the sister recovered shortly after, having been so gravely ill that she remembered neither her confession nor the Viaticum; whereas the Servant of God, a few days later, did indeed die.

§ 25
Holy death of the Servant of God.

Ad 22: I recall that the Servant of God died in the year 1885, of fever, in the house of the Briuccia Palace, top floor, in the room to the right as one enters. The illness lasted only a few days, during which the Servant of God did not belie her virtue: she received the Holy Sacraments of the Church amid the deep emotion of the Community.

§ 26
Funeral of the Servant of God.
§ 27
Request for relics.

Ad 23: The Servant of God's body, as soon as she died, was laid out in the Institute's chapel, if I recall rightly; and on the third day her funeral was held in that same Chapel, attended by a very select number of people, not only ordinary folk but also ladies. On that occasion the late V.le Gaetano Gabriele read a funeral oration, in which he recalled the Servant of God's virtues. Many people asked for relics of her. Beyond that I recall nothing more. As for her burial, she was interred in the Cemetery of St. Ursula.

§ 28
After her death, moved to a place of deposit.

Ad 24: I said that the Servant of God's body was buried in the Cemetery of St. Ursula, and afterwards the body was identified and placed in a place of deposit.

§ 29
Reputation for holiness in life.

Ad 26: I answer as above, that is, as at the beginning; I mean that, in life, she enjoyed a reputation for holiness because of her virtues, among those who had known her either closely or by repute.

Ad 27: After her death, the fame of the holiness of her life continued. More than this I cannot say.

Et expleto examine super Interrogatoriis, deventum est ad examen super Articulis, testis respondit:

§ 30
Humility practiced in the office of Provincial.

Ad 15, proc. p. 124: When the Servant of God returned from the General Chapter in Piacenza to Palermo — where for some years she had been Superior in the house of the nurse-sisters — bearing the office of Provincial, out of humility she kept the matter hidden for as long as she could, and I learned of it from the Mother House, from where I was written to. I can say she exercised the office of Provincial with true zeal, charity, and fortitude, never failing, as the need arose, to undertake difficult journeys and frequent hardships.

Ad 16: According to the depositions I made in the Interrogatories, the truth of this Article is made manifest.

§ 31
Serenity amid sufferings of spirit.

Ad 30: Despite her outward composure, a deep suffering of spirit showed through in the Servant of God.

Ad 31: I confirm the state of calm the Servant of God preserved at the extremity of her life.

§ 32
Charity towards God.

Ad 36: All this was related to me, while she lived, by the Sisters.

Ad 39: I heard that all this happened at the moment she received the Blessed Viaticum.

§ 33
Temperance.

Ad 67: I confirm this Article in all its particulars, as heard from the Sisters; as for the saying, "I have always been a little beast," I heard it myself from her own lips. On one occasion, when I remarked on her food, she once answered me: "But, Father, these things are not necessary," referring even to ordinary foods.

Ad 68: I fully confirm this Article as something I know to be true.

§ 34
On voluntary penances.

Ad 70: I have nothing to say against this Article. She used to say: "When the Sisters wish to do penance, they can procure mortifications for themselves; the community must do things in an orderly way."

Ad 71: I confirm this fact, which, moreover, was certainly not the only one, I myself having witnessed similar facts.

§ 35
Ardent desire for penance.

Ad 72: I know of the fact of the little chain found on the floor, as narrated by the Sisters. But I had occasion to know of the ardent desire the Servant of God had to use instruments of penance.

Ad 73: I recall having seen her, at times, bent and drawn, like a suffering person, although she strove to show her usual cheerfulness.

§ 36
Poverty.

Ad 75: I confirm this Article, as it is known to me personally from her stay in Palermo.

Ad 78: Most true, this fact, having been related to me, when it happened, by the Servant of God herself.

§ 37
Chastity.

Ad 82: Of this most penitential life, mention has already been made elsewhere.

§ 38
Prompt docility in obedience.

Ad 88: All this is most true; indeed I add that, a benefactor, namely Msgr. Briuccia, in whose palace the Community was lodged, having sent her, in her grave state of health, a quarter of a young chicken, she turned to me saying: "Father, I cannot possibly take this food." I understood she said this because she did not eat meat, having always abstained from it. I answered: "Let it be." But she added: "But Msgr. Briuccia will ask me about it, and if I do not taste it he might take it amiss." I then replied: "You may take a little morsel, to please him." She made a gesture of resignation with her hands and eyes. Having returned later, I asked her whether she had taken the chicken, and she answered: "I took it; it has gone in, but it will not come out again." She having died shortly after, I understood the meaning of her words.

§ 39
Humility.

Ad 91: For the time I knew her, I have nothing to say against it.

Ad 93: It seems to me I heard this expression of hers, even while she was Superior, addressed to other people.

§ 40
Gifts and miracles in life.

Ad 100: I know that she had the habit of placing monetary offerings behind the Altar Card, but this fact was never related to me, or at least I do not recall having heard of it.

§ 41
On her precious death.

Ad 110: I recall this fact in general: as for its particulars, I refer to what I said in the Interrogatories.

Ad 117: I confirm this Article; indeed I add that I there sang the solemn Requiem Mass as a Canon.

Ad 119: This Article is true: and I recall having been present at this fact.

§ 42
Reputation for holiness after death.

Ad 120-121: Most true, I confirm these Articles.

§ 43
Miracles after death.

Ad 125: I heard this fact related: but I gave it no importance, since Mr. Florio was accustomed to do so.

Ad 130: This fact was related to me by her own lips: but I would not know how to assess it, bearing in mind the nature of the illness.

Sister ANNA BATTISTINA BERTUZZI
